section_summary: This section covers diplomatic, consular, and commercial correspondence from 1938 to 1939 regarding severe Japanese restrictions on American motion pictures, including import embargoes, frozen royalties, and tight foreign exchange controls during the Second Sino-Japanese War. It details negotiations conducted by the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America (MPPDA), local film representatives, and Japanese intermediary Hisaji Kubo to secure import permits and deferred remittance arrangements through the Yokohama Specie Bank. The files also document the formulation, legislative enactment by the Imperial Diet, and diplomatic analysis of Japan's Motion Picture Law of 1939 (Law No. 66), which established comprehensive state control over cinema production, censorship, and distribution. In addition, the section traces requests for U.S. government educational visual materials and diplomatic representations to resolve customs blockades on American films at Yokohama.

subfiles.about: A report on the deteriorating situation for American motion pictures in Japan, detailing import embargoes, proposed quota restrictions, exchange controls, and the film monopoly in Manchukuo.

subfiles.summary: Tokyo report: the foreign film embargo is extended to April 1, 1938, a quota of 100 films is considered favoring Italy and Germany, exchange controls block remittances, and Manchukuo's film monopoly struggles.

subfiles.about: Transmitting the text of an international radio broadcast advocating balanced trade, import concessions for American motion pictures, and bilateral economic cooperation.
subfiles.from: Hisaji Kubo
subfiles.summary: Hisaji Kubo transmits to President Franklin D. Roosevelt the text of an international radio address delivered to the United States on December 1, 1938, over station JOAK in Tokyo. Kubo outlines his economic theory that international trade balance should be achieved through mutual tariff adjustments rather than import restrictions, citing the exchange of Japanese raw silk for American cotton as a model. He recounts his negotiations with American film executives in New York and Japanese authorities, which resulted in permission for major American companies to import films on three-year credit terms. Kubo explains Japanese trade restrictions as measures of self-preservation caused by the Sino-Japanese conflict and appeals for American understanding and commercial cooperation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hisaji Kubo to President Franklin D. Roosevelt Enclosing Radio Address on American Film Imports and Trade
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt

subfiles.about: Reporting on the draft Motion Picture Law submitted to the Imperial Diet, with an analysis of its control provisions and an English translation of the text.
subfiles.from: Charles R. Cameron, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Consul General Charles R. Cameron submits a detailed report on the draft Motion Picture Law introduced by the Japanese government to the Imperial Diet. The report explains that the measure establishes comprehensive state control over cinema production, distribution, exhibition, foreign film quotas, and mandatory registration of film personnel, consolidating import, exchange, and police powers under the Home Ministry. Cameron notes that the legislation creates a Motion Picture Commission and imposes penal sanctions for violations. Enclosed is an English translation of the 26 articles and supplementary rules of the draft law as published in the Official Gazette on March 10, 1939.
subfiles.title: Report No. 51: Proposed Motion Picture Law for Japan (with Draft Law Translation)
subfiles.to: Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Comprehensive economic and political report on the promulgated Motion Picture Law (Law No. 66), corporate rivalries, import and remittance restrictions, and market conditions, enclosing a translation of the law.
subfiles.from: Charles R. Cameron, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Consul General Charles R. Cameron presents a detailed report on the Motion Picture Law (Law No. 66, promulgated April 4, 1939) and broader developments in the Japanese cinema trade. The report discusses pending Imperial enforcement ordinances, the import of roughly 120 American films under the August 1938 agreement, the remittance of 3,000,000 yen in royalties alongside 2,000,000 yen remaining frozen, and intense corporate competition between the Toho and Shochiku theatrical combines for control of Nikkatsu. It highlights raw film shortages, box office popularity of American aviation features ("Test Pilot" and "Hurricane"), and expanding exhibition markets in Korea and Formosa. A confidential section notes that Japanese authorities permit American films to maintain domestic civilian morale, provide plot material for local studios, and discourage anti-Japanese propaganda in Hollywood. Enclosed is a corrected English translation of Law No. 66.
subfiles.title: Report No. 59: Japan Motion Picture Law (with Translation of Law No. 66)
subfiles.to: Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Transmitting records of meetings with American film distributors in Tokyo, their formal statement of grievances against the Finance Ministry, and a critical analysis of questionable financial arrangements involving Hisaji Kubo and former Finance Minister Kaya.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on a conference held on November 13, 1939, between Embassy officers and eight representatives of the American Motion Picture Association of Japan (representing MGM, Warner Bros., 20th Century-Fox, RKO, Paramount, Universal, United Artists, and Columbia). The distributors sought Embassy intercession to release $10,000 worth of American films held in the Yokohama Custom House under an August 1938 arrangement that permitted $30,000 in imports and 3,000,000 yen in remittances. Grew notes that the arrangement was merely an informal letter of expectation and critically highlights that the association paid a 30,000 yen gratuity to Hisaji Kubo, an intermediary closely connected to former Finance Minister O. Kaya, who reportedly profited during his tenure. Enclosures include Edward S. Crocker's memorandum of the November 13 conversation and the association's formal letter of November 16 outlining their grievances and negotiation history.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4259: Difficulties Encountered by the American Motion Picture Association of Japan (with Enclosures)
subfiles.to: Secretary of State
